title: 25. Every Body Is Beautiful and Sexy
subtitle: Out of comparison, into feeling: how women and men can see their bodies with kind eyes and feel desirable in them.

lessons.title: The Myth of the Perfect Body
lessons.summary: Where the idea of the “right” body comes from, and how varied the bodies of women and men really are.
lessons.content:
Most of the bodies we see every day have been carefully selected, well lit and often edited. In advertising, on social media, in films and in porn, they show only a tiny slice of what people actually look like. Anyone who measures themselves against that can only lose. That's as true for women as it is for men, even though the ideals differ.

Two ideals, one problem
Women are often shown a slim, firm, smooth body: a flat belly, firm breasts, not a trace of cellulite, no hair except on the head. Men are often shown a tall, muscular body: broad shoulders, a six-pack, full hair, a big penis. Both ideals have one thing in common: very few people look like that, and even they often only with good lighting, the right pose and photo editing.

How varied bodies really are
Skin: it has pores, moles, freckles, spots, redness, scars and stretch marks, in women and men alike. The vast majority of women have cellulite, including very slim women.
Hair: everyone grows body hair, sometimes thick, sometimes sparse, on the legs, armpits, belly, chest, back and around the genitals. Many men lose hair on their head over the years; that's very common and not a weakness.
Belly and bottom: bellies are round, soft, and have folds or rolls when you sit. Bottoms are flat or round, firm or soft.
Chest: breasts differ in size and shape, often even the two breasts of the same woman. Nipples are light or dark, large or small, flat or protruding. Men have a chest too, which can be flat, muscular or soft.
Height and build: bodies are tall or short, narrow or broad, sturdy or slight. None of these shapes is naturally more attractive than another.
Genitals: labia can be short or long, and the two sides are usually different. Penises are straight or curved. When soft they are sometimes smaller, sometimes larger, and that says little about how big they get when aroused. Testicles often hang at different heights.
All of this is normal, not the exception.

Why comparison hurts so much
Our brain compares automatically. Seeing lots of edited images quietly shifts our inner yardstick. At some point your own, perfectly normal body starts to look like a mistake. So the problem isn't your body, it's the yardstick you measure it against.
On top of that: anyone who struggles with how they look is often half in their head during sex. Instead of feeling, they watch themselves. That costs pleasure, which is exactly why it's worth changing this way of looking.

The task
For one week, notice which body images you come across: on your phone, in ads, in films. Each time, briefly ask yourself: is this real or staged? And what feeling does this image stir in me?
If you like, also follow a few people or projects that show real, unedited bodies, of women and of men. Many find that this changes how they see themselves, too.
lessons.reflection_question: Which image of a “right” body do you carry around with you, and where does it come from?

lessons.title: A Kind Look in the Mirror
lessons.summary: Describing instead of judging: a mirror exercise for women and men that quietens the inner critic.
lessons.content:
Many people look in the mirror like a strict inspector: what's wrong, what's too much, what's too little? For women this gaze often lands on the belly, thighs, bottom and skin. For men on the belly, muscles, height, hairline and penis. This critical gaze is learned, and it can be unlearned too.

Describing instead of judging
The first step isn't to find everything beautiful. That would be asking too much. The first step is to look neutrally. Experts call this body neutrality: seeing your body as it is, without judgement.
Instead of “my belly is too fat”, you say: “My belly is round and soft.”
Instead of “my thighs are awful”: “My thighs are strong and carry me.”
Instead of “I hardly have any muscles”: “My arms are slim.”
Instead of “my hair is getting thin”: “My hair is shorter and lighter than it used to be.”
Neutrality is a bridge between rejection and affection. Once you stop putting yourself down, there's room for kindness.

The task
Stand in front of a mirror for ten minutes, clothed or naked, whatever feels right for you. Make sure the light is pleasant and nobody will disturb you.
Let your gaze wander slowly from top to bottom: hair, face, neck, shoulders, chest, arms, hands, belly, hips, bottom, genitals, thighs, knees, calves, feet. Describe each part in one neutral sentence, out loud or silently.
When a judgement comes up, notice it without condemning yourself for it, and rephrase it neutrally.
Finally, name three things you like about your body and three things you're grateful to it for. For example: my hands can be tender. My legs carried me to work today. My skin feels every touch.

If it's hard
That's normal, especially at first. Start with five minutes. Repeat the exercise a few days in a row. Many notice after a week that the inner critic gets quieter and they pick at themselves less in everyday life.
If looking in the mirror weighs on you heavily, for example if you spend hours preoccupied with one body part or withdraw because of it, talk to a doctor or a psychotherapist. There's good help for this.

Going deeper
The guided body journey below this lesson continues the exercise with your hands: feeling instead of looking.
lessons.reflection_question: Which neutral sentence about your body felt surprisingly good?

lessons.title: Sexy Is a Feeling, Not a Measurement
lessons.summary: What attraction really is about, and how women and men can feel desirable in their bodies.
lessons.content:
Who we find attractive depends surprisingly little on measurements. Presence, a look, a laugh, a voice, the way someone moves and how someone smells: those are the things people remember. And the most important part: feeling sexy is something you can learn, regardless of dress size, height or muscles.

What attraction is about
Many people say they fell in love with someone who wasn't their “type” at all. Attraction arises in contact: when someone feels seen, when someone is relaxed and genuine, when there's humour and warmth. Self-assurance often has a stronger effect than any detail of the body. And self-assurance doesn't mean finding yourself perfect, it means not constantly hiding.

What makes you feel sexy
For some it's a particular piece of clothing: lace, a well-fitting shirt, jeans you feel good in. For others music, dancing, a scent, freshly washed hair, a well-groomed beard or simply a well-rested morning. For some it's movement: sport, yoga, a walk after which you can feel your own muscles.
It isn't about how you look to others, but about how you feel in your body.

The task
Write a list of five things that make you feel sexy or alive. Choose two and do them deliberately this week, just for you. A few ideas:
Wear underwear that feels good, even if nobody sees it.
Dance in the kitchen to a song that moves you.
Take time for body care: lotion, shaving or deliberately not shaving, a warm bath.
Walk more upright for a day, with a soft belly, relaxed shoulders and an open chest.
Look at a photo of yourself where you liked how you looked, and ask yourself what you felt back then.

The body thinks along
Posture and feeling are linked. Standing tall, letting your shoulders drop and breathing deep into your belly often changes how you feel inside too. Sucking in your belly and holding your breath, on the other hand, keeps you tense. Try both deliberately and notice what they do to you.

For couples
For one week, give each other a compliment about the other's body every day, and make it concrete: not “you look good”, but “I love how your shoulders look when you stretch”. Whoever receives the compliment just says “thank you”, without playing it down.
lessons.reflection_question: Which of the five things on your list makes you feel most like yourself?

lessons.title: Lights On: Letting Go of Shame in Bed
lessons.summary: When the light has to go off or the blanket has to stay on: how women and men can quieten shame together.
lessons.content:
Many people can only half enjoy sex because part of their attention is somewhere else. Women suck in their belly, hold on to the blanket or avoid positions in which they find their body “unflattering”. Men worry whether their penis is big enough, whether the erection will last, whether their belly is in the way, or whether they look too hairy or not muscular enough in the light. This self-watching costs arousal. The less you watch yourself, the more you can feel.

What really counts
Often your partner pays attention to completely different things than you do: to closeness, to desire and to you letting go. The belly you see so critically is often simply part of the person they desire. Many people say their partner's insecurity bothers them more than any supposed problem zone, because they want the other to feel good.

Talking about it
Shame gets quieter when you say it out loud. In a calm moment, not in bed, tell each other which parts of your body make you feel insecure. Then the other says what they like about exactly these parts, or simply find normal. Listening is enough, without contradicting or sugar-coating.

The task for two
Take an evening with warm, dimmed light. Undress each other slowly. Whoever is undressing says one sentence with each piece of clothing about what they find beautiful or attractive about the part that's just been revealed. Whoever is being undressed says nothing except “thank you”. Then you swap.
When you're both naked, lie down next to each other and stroke each other for a few minutes with just your eyes and fingertips, without a goal.

If it's too much
Start smaller: candlelight instead of the ceiling lamp, a shirt that may stay on, or one part per evening. There's no obligation to have the light on. There's only the invitation to show a little more of yourselves, bit by bit.

For singles
The exercise also works alone in front of the mirror: undress slowly and give each part that's revealed a kind sentence. And for the next time with someone new, this thought may help: nobody expects a perfect body, only a person who is truly present.
lessons.reflection_question: What surprised you most about what your partner finds beautiful about you?

lessons.title: When Your Body Changes
lessons.summary: Pregnancy, ageing, illness, scars: how women and men can stay kind to their bodies, even as they change.
lessons.content:
No body stays the same. Life leaves its marks, on women and on men. Sometimes your own body feels foreign afterwards, and that can affect desire too.

What can change
For women: after pregnancy, the belly, breasts and skin often change, and stretch marks or a caesarean scar remain. During menopause, skin, weight, hair and vaginal moisture change.
For men: over the years, hair on the head often thins, the belly gets rounder, the muscles get softer. Erections take more time or more direct touch. After prostate surgery or with some medications, erection and ejaculation can change.
For everyone: weight changes, operations, accidents, chronic illnesses, breast surgery, a stoma, scars and skin changes. And simply ageing, with wrinkles, age spots and grey hair.

Grief is allowed
If you miss a body you used to have, that's allowed. Forbidding yourself this grief or brushing it off with “just be grateful” doesn't help. Acknowledging it often clears the way to making friends with the body you have today.

Your body has been through something
A scar tells of an operation that helped. A belly of a child it carried. Wrinkles of many years of laughing. Grey hair of a life that has been lived. You don't have to find that beautiful. But you can acknowledge what your body has carried and come through.

Desire changes, it doesn't disappear
Many couples discover new forms of closeness precisely after changes: more time, more touch across the whole body, less fixation on the same old routine. Those who stay curious often find paths they never had in view before.

The task
Place a hand on a part that has changed or that you struggle with. Breathe calmly into it a few times. Say silently: “Thank you for carrying me through all of this.” If it feels right, stroke it slowly with a little oil. If you're in a relationship, you can invite your partner to touch this part together with you.

Good to know
Changes can affect sexuality too, for example altered sensation after an operation, dryness during menopause or erection problems. Much of this can be treated well, for example with lubricants, local hormones, medication or pelvic floor training. Talk to a doctor if something is weighing on you. It isn't an embarrassing topic, it's everyday business in any practice.
lessons.reflection_question: What can you thank your body for today, even if you don't like everything about it?

lessons.title: Wrapped up: lingerie for every body
lessons.summary: Sexy lingerie isn't just for models: how women and men find underwear they like themselves in.
lessons.content:
Sexy lingerie has a reputation, as if it were made only for young, slim women who look like the ads. Yet it is there for every body: for women and men, for every size and every age. Good lingerie doesn't hide a body, it frames it. And most importantly: it should feel good to you first.

Why lingerie can change so much
What we wear on our skin changes how we move and how we feel. Many people say that in beautiful underwear they walk differently, sit up straighter and look at themselves more kindly in the mirror. That holds true even when nobody else sees it.

For women
There is much more than the classic push-up bra. Soft bralettes without underwire, bodysuits that flatter the whole upper body, camisoles of silk or satin, high-cut briefs that make the legs look longer, lace, mesh, stockings with suspenders. Good shops and brands offer lingerie in many sizes, including for large breasts, wide hips and round bellies. Many women with a soft belly feel especially good in high-waisted briefs or a bodysuit. Others love to show their belly.

For men
Men have more options than grey boxer shorts, too. Snug trunks, skimpy briefs, underwear made of mesh or sheer fabric, silk shorts, an open shirt over bare skin. For many men the thought of dressing up for their partner is unfamiliar. Yet many partners find exactly that very attractive: that he makes an effort and wants to show himself.

How to find what suits you
The size: underwear that pinches or cuts in doesn't feel sexy. Get advice or measure yourself. Sizes vary a lot from brand to brand.
The fabric: silk and satin are cool and smooth, lace is playful, cotton is soft, mesh is cheeky. Touch the fabric and imagine how it will feel for a whole evening.
The colour: black and red are classics. Dark green, burgundy, midnight blue or a shade close to your skin tone can be just as beautiful.
Your favourite spot: which part of yourself do you like? Your bottom, your back, your shoulders, your chest, your legs? Look for lingerie that shows off exactly that spot.

The exercise
Pick a piece of lingerie you would never normally buy and try it on, in the shop or at home in front of the mirror. Don't pay attention to what bothers you, but to what it does to your posture. Then wear it for a whole day under your normal clothes. Nobody needs to know.

For couples
Choose lingerie together, in a shop or on the sofa. Each person picks one piece for themselves and one for the other. Anyone who doesn't want to wear something says so, and it isn't up for discussion. And don't forget the men: he gets to be wrapped up nicely, too.
lessons.reflection_question: Which piece of lingerie surprised you by how good you felt in it, and which part of you did it show off?
